note: RI-DLG01 §How-we-lose: 'One INFO per topic. No filter stack at all — every NPC gives the same answer.' Morrowind's Balmora answers the SAME murder question three ways by race. Every settlement node below carries at least three filtered answers for that reason.

infos.x: There was a well here. The sunken well is under the water now and it is still tended. People swim down to it once a season, supplicant, and come up with nothing, and go again the next season, because the covenant does not lapse when a thing goes under. I have never been able to call that either faith or stubbornness.

It's the only town in the province where a person can sleep dry for nothing, dry-one, if you don't count the boards. There are that many rooms nobody's ever claimed down in the low city. And every one of them is spoken for, if you ask the wrong person.

Lilmoth. Two cities, friend. Take the tide steps down past the low city and the drowned quarter is under your feet, and it still has people in it. This one doesn't go down there after dark. Are you staying long?
Port city. Six thousand. Half of them off the rolls. We hold the harbour chain and the stair. Below that is the low city, and the low city belongs to the Wet Ledger.

The colonial city was built on the made ground and the ground has been unmaking itself for two centuries; what is under it now is the drowned quarter. The survey puts the rate at a hand a decade. The survey began after the first floor had already gone, which is a difficulty for the imperial claim and for nobody else.

They call it the low city because it is low, dry-one. The roof walks above it got called the high city as a joke. Then everyone forgot it was a joke. Now people put on airs about which one they live on.
Second floors and the roof walks. Everything happens up there. Under it all is the drowned quarter. Friend, the ground floor is for water. Have you got a bed yet?
Planks across the old roofs, the boards but higher. Faster than a boat. They come down at the second stair. Friend, mind the third span, it's gone. Do you want me to walk you across?
Everything goes past the customs man and everything is contraband to him. Friend, not everything comes ashore at a stair, and the second stair is not one he watches.
Landing stair, under the harbour chain. Customs post at the top. Everything off a boat goes past me. The manifest or nothing. Where's yours?
Under it, at the low tide. Friend, that is where the organ market is, and the cut is the way out of it. Ask nothing. Point at things.
Old stair. Condemned. It isn't used. Move along, citizen!

Raised at dusk. Dropped at dawn. And it has not been raised in two years. Winch is rotten, the requisition the quartermaster wrote was refused, and the money that would mend it goes out as the dead pay.

A harbour chain is a statement about who may leave, not who may enter, and this one is generally acknowledged to be inoperable. I would call that the single most eloquent document in the province on the condition of the imperial claim, and it is not a document at all.

Rubble, ballast and the demolished first city, tipped into the shallows and built on; the drowned quarter is what is left of it and the sunken well is under that. It was an entirely standard Imperial procedure. It had worked in a dozen other provinces. In none of those was the substrate silt over nothing.

It is not dead and it is not reachable, supplicant, and it is not counted among the quiet wells for that reason. The swimmers go down once a season and every one of them comes up saying the same thing. They say it is still asking, and the covenant does not permit us to stop answering.

Four of them go down to the sunken well. They are not keepers and they were never given to a well. They go anyway, once a season, because it must be done, and Hides His Foot is the eldest of them. The order has never decided whether to thank them or to stop them, supplicant, and I have stopped waiting for it to.

They go down at the turn, and they come up grey, and they don't talk for a day after, dry-one. Hides His Foot is the one who still will. And one year one of them didn't come up. The others went back the next season anyway.

He is the oldest of the swimmers and he has been going down into the sunken well since before the fever, dry-one. If you want him, he is on the third of the roof walks in the afternoon with his back to the water. He always sits that way.
Oldest of the swimmers. Buys nothing. Sells nothing. Friend, this one respects that.

They tax the lamps, so half the roof walks are dark now, dry-one. And the dark ones are where a person gets pushed off a plank at night, into the cut. Nobody has to explain that to anyone. I don't walk them.
A drake a month per lamp on the roof walks. It pays for the oil. It doesn't pay for the oil, and the Provincial Office has never once been asked where the rest of it goes.

When it closes there's a half hour where the boxes get turned out onto the boards, dry-one. Nobody minds who's standing there. I've eaten better in that half hour than most people manage on a wage, and I'll not pretend otherwise.
Dawn only, at the foot of the tide steps. Buy at the third bell. Friend, before that you're paying for the noise. Are you buying or selling?
Runs the organ market at the second stair. Never touches the goods. Friend, twelve years and never once touched them. Do you want an introduction?
Known. Nothing on her, and nothing on the organ market either. Twelve years of nothing on her.
Behind them is the cut. Friend, things go in the front and out the back and only one of those is written down, and the short weight is how the difference gets spelled.
Every door of it belongs to the Wet Ledger. Backs onto the cut. We knock. We do not go in. Why are you asking, citizen?

There is no well here and there never was, supplicant. The salt hills hold no water worth the covenant. So the Empire could build here and there was no argument to be had. No keeper has ever been posted to Stormhold.
Good town to beg in, dry-one. Bad town to sleep in. The streets are dry and full of people with coin. The night watch walks them all night for exactly that reason.
Border garrison. The wall street, the gate fee, the muster board and the market. Four streets. Cleanest town in the province. What's your business here, citizen?

Stormhold is the only settlement in Argonia laid out to an Imperial plan and completed to it, and the effect on a traveller arriving from the interior is genuinely disorienting. A right-angled town on the dry rock of the salt hills, with the drains laid to the plan and still working, twelve hours from a place where the ground has opinions.
The gate fee, the market fee, and the weigh house takes a third. Friend, Stormhold charges for air. How long are you in for?
Runs the inside of the wall. Barracks, the quartermaster, wall house. Ancus Varo is at the far end of it and so is everything the Ninth Cohort owns. And don't wander!
Every cart, every load, one drake a stone. Friend, the scales belong to the Wet Ledger and the fee belongs to the Empire, and the short weight belongs to neither.

The arrangement is unusual and it has never been examined. The Empire levies the duty, the Ledger owns the instrument that determines the duty, and the Provincial Office receives a figure it has no independent means of checking. The short weight is the predictable consequence. I have put that in writing twice.

They'll move you on off the boards four times a night without ever once being cruel about it, dry-one. And by the fourth time you've walked further than a man does in a day's work, and you haven't slept.
Two on each street. Dusk to fourth bell. Lantern, horn, cudgel. No blades on the watch, and the sanction for one of us is the same as for you.

Cut into the salt hills by the original engineers and still functioning, the under drain included. No other Imperial infrastructure in Argonia is. They are holes in stone and there is nothing in them to rot.

There's a grating on the north side of the drains that has been unbolted and bolted again, dry-one. I know it has, because I slept against it for a winter, and the bolts were rusted and now two of them are bright. The night watch never goes near it, and Belena Sarn walks that street twice a week. And men don't polish bolts for nothing.
Storm drain, the last of the drains on the north side. Sealed. Nothing down there but salt.
North to Morrowind. Twelve miles of it is ours. After that it is the slavers road, and it belongs to House Dres, and it is worse.
Good stone, the best of the cart roads. Bad company. Friend, this one goes in daylight only. Are you going north?
Salt, hide, dried fish, iron, and every load of it through the weigh house. No sap. Friend, no sap in this town at all since the quiet wells. Have you seen any north of the ford?

The absence of sap in the Stormhold market is recent, and supply does not explain it, since the routes still run and the quiet wells were never on them. What has changed is that the Wet Ledger has stopped offering it here, and the Ledger does not stop offering a profitable thing for reasons it publishes.
The man the Wet Ledger keeps at the weigh house. Polite. Very polite. Friend, that isn't a compliment.

He's given me coin twice, and both times he asked me afterwards what I had seen that week, dry-one, and the second time he asked about the under drain by name. I did not understand until then that the coin was for the answer and not for me. The Wet Ledger pays him and he pays me.

Helstrom is not a city with a tree in it. It is the Great Hist, which has been permitted to have a city. The root halls are its rooms and the covenant is its law. Everything you find strange about the place follows from that one sentence, supplicant, and from nothing else. Say it back to me before you go in.
No cart goes in. The carriers take everything in on their backs, into the root halls. Friend, this one has never been past the second root. Have you been asked in?
Were House Dres permitted a factor in Helstrom, provincial, it would have one. It is not permitted. It never has been. Every other town in this province has a Dres factor in it.

No Imperial survey of Helstrom has ever been completed and the root halls appear on none of them. The three attempts are catalogued as abandoned rather than refused, alongside the unfinished survey of the east. The Office has maintained that distinction for a hundred and forty years. It has never said what the surveyors encountered.
We keep an outpost. Outside. By arrangement. And don't ask what the arrangement is, citizen.

The halls are the spaces the Great Hist left behind it. They are not cut and they are not shaped. A person who lives in one has been given it, and the given halls are given at the naming and not after. A person who is given one is expected to be worth the gift for the rest of their life. Mine was given to me at nine and I am still being measured against it.

Chambers formed by root growth, occupied without modification, and allocated by a process no Imperial observer has described in under a page or with any confidence at all. The given halls, they are called. I have read four such attempts and they contradict each other.

It is not inherited. It is not bought. It is not earned in the way you mean, supplicant. The well is asked, the Great Hist answers, and the covenant holds whoever it names. The answer has been wrong twice in living memory. Both times the person was left in the hall anyway, and Naheesh-Tul will tell you she did not vote for that either.

The eldest of the keepers here, and she is not in authority over anyone. She holds one of the given halls, she has counted every one of the quiet wells, and she was standing there when the arrangement was made. Every Imperial visitor refuses to believe she commands nothing. They come with a proposal and there is no one to put it to.
The old one, deep in the root halls. Sees all comers. Sells nothing. Friend, go with clean hands. Do you know what you'll ask her?

The Empire was told it could keep twenty soldiers where they could be seen, and it agreed, and Naheesh-Tul was standing there when it did. It has never once understood that being visible was the entire content of the concession, and the imperial claim rests on that misunderstanding here more than anywhere else.
Twenty men of the Ninth Cohort. Outside the third root. We do not go into the root halls. They do not come out. Twelve years, no incident.

There is no instrument. I have looked, including in the Blackwater Treaty, which would have been the place for it. Whatever governs the Cohort's presence at Helstrom was agreed verbally, is honoured absolutely by both parties, and does not exist in any register in Cyrodiil.
It's the one trade here a stranger can get, dry-one, and it will break your back in four years. For those four years you are inside the root halls every day. Some people think that's worth a back.
No wheels past the gate, so the cart roads stop there. They carry it all into the root halls on their backs. Friend, they charge by the root, not the mile. What are you carrying?

It is the root the Empire is permitted to stand beside under the arrangement. It is also the root that has been six years in the thinning, and the quiet wells began in the same season. I do not say those facts are connected, supplicant. I say only that I have watched people decide they are, and that I did not correct them.

Six years on the third root, and it is not cutting, and it is not the Empire, and it is not the fever. I have eliminated those in that order over six years, and Naheesh-Tul has eliminated the quiet wells and the bad dreams as causes rather than as symptoms. I am left with the answer I did not want. It is being asked for something, supplicant, and it is answering.

The sap yield from the Helstrom wells is down by a figure the Wet Ledger will not state, and which its own carriage bookings put at close to a third. The quiet wells account for none of it. Over six years, monotonically. That last word is the one that troubles me.

The eggs are tended in the fourth hall and they are tended by whoever is nearest, and not one of them is anyone's until the naming. The Empire records that as communal childrearing. It is not that at all, supplicant. Under the covenant it is that they are not anyone's.

Egg-tending is the single most misdescribed practice in the Imperial literature on this province, generally rendered as a quaint communalism. The sources available to any surveyor who had bothered to ask would establish that it is a legal status which ends at the naming, and that the status is 'unowned'. Nobody asked.

In the deepest hall the floor is the root of the Great Hist itself, and it carries sound from a very long way. Keepers lie on it. What is heard is not reported. Since the thinning began, those who lie on it have had the bad dreams worst of anyone. I will not tell you what I have heard on it, supplicant. I have not decided what it was.
Eldest of the carriers. Twenty years on the roots. Knows every one of the root halls, and he has lain on the listening floor. Friend, buy the first drink.
He carried for the keepers before he carried for the Wet Ledger, dry-one, and there aren't many of the carriers who have done both. And he won't say why he stopped doing the first.
